I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

vignette: Mr. Henry Kramer is a 76-year-old widowed European-American who was once a cashier at a local supermarket. At age 35, he served as a civilian in a war zone during his late twenties and early thirties, an experience that continues to haunt him today. The traumatic event unfolded when Mr. Kramer's convoy was ambushed while driving through a narrow mountain pass. He vividly recalls the sound of gunfire, the smell of smoke, and the sight of comrades falling from their vehicles. The suddenness and violence of the attack left a profound impact on his psyche. Since that day, he has avoided driving or even being a passenger in any vehicle, finding the idea too reminiscent of the ambush and its aftermath. Mr. Kramer's maladaptive strategies have become deeply ingrained over time. He often finds himself thinking about why this event happened to him, seeking meaning in the chaos and devastation. This constant introspection has led him to push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe. He believes that dwelling on happy moments only reminds him of how fragile life can be, a stark contrast to his current state of hypervigilance. Henry's heightened sense of threat is evident in his daily interactions. He remains superalert and watchful at all times, constantly scanning the environment for any potential dangers. At work, he notices every slight movement or sound made by customers, leading him to believe that they might pose a threat. This hypervigilance has extended to his sleep as well; he often struggles to fall asleep because he feels he needs to stay alert. When Mr. Kramer recalls the event, it is often through vivid visual memories that feel like they are happening in the present moment. Sometimes, these recollections come without any emotional charge, leaving him feeling numb and disconnected from his own experiences as if they happened to a stranger. These intrusive images intrude at unexpected times, disrupting his daily routine and causing significant distress. Over time, Mr. Kramer has developed negative appraisals that shape his view of the world and himself. He believes that the world is inherently dangerous and that he is no longer capable of doing the things that once defined him as a capable and resilient individual. The loss of faith in people, life, and higher powers further compounds his sense of isolation and vulnerability. Mr. Kramer's maladaptive behaviors have had tangible consequences on his daily life. His avoidance of driving has limited his ability to go out alone, leading to increased dependency on friends and family for transportation. This reliance has strained relationships, as he often feels like a burden. At work, his hypervigilance and constant monitoring of customers can be perceived as intrusive or overly cautious by coworkers and management. What finally brought Mr. Kramer to seek help was a recent incident where he became overwhelmed during an event that reminded him of the ambush. He realized that he needed support to navigate these overwhelming feelings and regain control over his life. While he is most afraid of losing himself entirely to these intrusive thoughts and memories, he also hopes for a return to some semblance of normalcy and peace. Mr. Kramer's journey towards recovery will involve addressing his maladaptive strategies, reducing hypervigilance, and finding ways to process the traumatic event without feeling overwhelmed by its images and emotions. He seeks a path where he can reclaim faith in people and life itself, allowing him to reconnect with the world around him in a meaningful way.
